cues.text: Chapter nine is the final consolidation.
This is where we stop adding new material and make sure the earlier ideas work together, so you can use them when a question or a real business problem arrives.
The source gives one instruction for this chapter.

Know the three digital maturity terms, the innovation categories, the seven layers, IT and business alignment, infrastructure choices, strategic value, competitive advantage, barriers, and success and failure lessons.
Then apply each one to a concrete business outcome, rather than memorising technology brand names.
That last sentence is the key to the whole chapter.
An examiner, or a manager, rarely wants a product name.
They want to know what changed for the business, and why.
Start with the three digital maturity terms: digitisation, digitalisation and digital transformation.
They describe three different depths of change.
Digitisation is converting something analogue into a digital form.
A paper register becomes a scanned file, or a handwritten ledger becomes a spreadsheet.
The information is the same, and only its format has changed.
Digitalisation is using digital technology to change how a process works.
Once the register is digital, you might route it automatically to the right person for approval, so the work itself runs differently.
Digital transformation is the deepest level.
It changes the organisation itself: its strategy, its way of creating value, its structure, its culture and how it serves customers.
It is much more than adopting new tools.
Here is an illustration.
It is a teaching example, not evidence from the source.
Imagine a Nigerian retailer that scans its paper sales books.
That is digitisation.
It then connects sales to automatic stock reordering, which is digitalisation.
Finally, it uses customer data to redesign what it sells, how it prices and how it reaches customers.
That is digital transformation.
The business outcome at each step is different: easier record keeping, then faster and more efficient operations, then a changed way of competing.
Next, the innovation categories and the seven layers.
The source tells you to know both, and the exact categories and the seven layers are those set out earlier in your course notes.
Revise them in that original order and wording.
When you do, attach each one to an outcome by asking what it improves and for whom.
A category or layer you can tie to an outcome is one you can use in an answer.
A bare list is easy to forget.
Then comes IT and business alignment.
This means technology investment is driven by business goals, and the business understands what technology makes possible.
Without alignment, you get systems nobody needs, or business ambitions that the systems cannot support.
The outcome to look for is that technology spending measurably supports a stated business objective.
Infrastructure choices come next.
These are decisions about what technology foundation the organisation builds on, and how it obtains it.
When you answer, state the choice and then the trade-offs it brings, such as cost, control, flexibility and risk, because a choice only makes sense against what the business needs.
Do not defend an option just by naming a product.
Strategic value is the contribution technology makes to the organisation's goals, beyond simply keeping it running.
Competitive advantage is a position that lets the organisation perform better than rivals in a way that lasts.
The link between them is important.
Technology creates competitive advantage only when it delivers strategic value that rivals cannot easily copy.
Owning the same tools as everyone else rarely does that.
Barriers are the obstacles that slow or block digital change.
The source does not list them here, so recall them from your earlier chapters.
For each one, ask what business outcome it puts at risk.
This turns a list of barriers into a diagnosis you can act on.
Finally, success and failure lessons.
Look at what successful transformations had in common and what failed ones lacked.
Then test any case you meet against those same questions.
Was there a clear business outcome?
Was the technology aligned to strategy?
Were the barriers anticipated?
So here is a method for every topic in this chapter.
Define the term.
Link it to a business outcome.
Say what could go wrong.
If you can do those three things without relying on a brand name, you have understood the material.
